newsitem.title: USA: China seeks floating, liberalized currency.
newsitem.headline: China seeks floating, liberalized currency.

text.p: China's central bank chief said on Sunday that China does not intend to influence the exchange rate, and plans to eventually make its currency fully convertible.

"The exchange rate is determined by the market, not by the central bank or by the government," Dai Xianglong, governor of the People's Bank of China told Reuters Financial Television. "A fully convertible currency is our target."
While the China's current account is now fully convertible, the complete liberalisation of the capital accounts will take time, Dai said.

"It is very difficult for me to give you a timetable," Dai said. He noted that the central bank was operating cautiously to avoid any kind of currency crisis, such as occurred in Mexico in December 1994.
"With a foreign exchange surplus and increasing foreign exchange reserves we will not have a Mexico-type crisis if we are careful," Dai said.
He said that China's retail prices would rise by about 7.0 percent this year, below the original inflation targets, and that interest rates reflected the level of price pressures.
"Right now the interest rate is consistent with the price level," Dai said. In August, the central bank reduced interest rates in response to declining inflation.
With reserves nearing $100 billion, China is hesitant to enter the capital market with bond issues, Dai said.
The central banker also forecast a smooth financial transition when Hong Kong returns to Chinese governance next year.

"Because people are confident in Hong Kong, I don't imagine a large fluctuation in money flows in Hong Kong," he said. "Once it is transferred, I am confident there will be stability," he added, reaffirming the one country, two system approach to the territory.
"Hong Kong's status as a financial centre will not be undermined," Dai said. "Planned economic development will contribute to the stability of Hong Kong."
